This study investigates the spectroscopic properties of the $\Omega^{-}$ baryon, which carries a strangeness of -3. The analysis employs the light-front quark model to calculate the baryon's mass spectrum and electromagnetic form factors. The results indicate that the $\Omega^{-}$ mass is approximately 1660 MeV, aligning well with experimental data. Furthermore, the electromagnetic form factors exhibit a dipole behavior, and the charge radius is determined to be 0.42 fm.

This study evaluates the applicability of a well-mixed model for forecasting disease transmission on an urban bus. We compare the well-mixed approach against a spatially explicit framework that accounts for the physical layout of the vehicle. Our analysis indicates that the well-mixed model can accurately predict transmission rates when the number of passengers is high, whereas it tends to overestimate transmission when occupancy is low. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the well-mixed model remains effective for estimating the impact of interventions, such as mask usage and social distancing.

Quantum vacuum birefringence and diffraction are nonlinear optical phenomena arising from the interaction between light and the quantum vacuum. These effects are predicted by Quantum Electrodynamics (QED) and are expected to manifest in high-intensity laser experiments. This paper reviews the current experimental techniques used to detect these phenomena, with a specific focus on the proposed methods for observing quantum vacuum birefringence and diffraction.

This paper presents a new algorithm for determining the automorphism group of a polyhedron, specifically designed for the class of fully transitive structures. This method builds upon the foundational work of Eisenlohr and Farris, which originally addressed the case of flag-transitive polyhedra.

This paper introduces a new definition of uncloneable encryption, which is a cryptographic primitive designed to prevent adversaries from duplicating ciphertexts. We demonstrate that this primitive is achievable in the standard model and establish its connection to other cryptographic tools, specifically proving that uncloneable encryption implies the existence of a strong pseudorandom generator. Furthermore, we show that the primitive is secure against adversaries with quantum capabilities.

This work introduces a new authentication protocol for the additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channel, which relies on the inherent randomness of the noise itself. The method is designed to be secure against adversaries capable of eavesdropping and tampering with the channel, while requiring only a single bit of shared secret information between the transmitter and receiver. Furthermore, the protocol is proven to be secure against any adversary, regardless of their computational power.

We present a theoretical framework for investigating plasmons in twisted bilayer transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs), focusing on the flat-band regime. Our approach integrates a tight-binding model with a random-phase approximation (RPA) to derive the dielectric function, which is subsequently used to calculate plasmon dispersion relations. Our findings indicate that flat-band plasmons exist in twisted bilayer TMDs, exhibiting a linear dispersion relation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the plasmon energy can be tuned by varying the interlayer distance, thereby offering a viable mechanism for controlling plasmonic properties in these systems.

This study investigates the characteristics of almost conformal Ricci solitons within the framework of Sasakian manifolds. We establish that any such soliton existing on a Sasakian manifold is necessarily a gradient soliton. Furthermore, we demonstrate that if the potential function of a gradient almost conformal Ricci soliton on a Sasakian manifold is constant, the structure becomes an Einstein manifold. Finally, we derive specific traits regarding almost conformal Ricci solitons on Sasakian space forms.

The study of stellar winds and magnetospheres has long been a cornerstone of astrophysics, while planetary magnetospheres and atmospheres have only recently gained comparable attention. This review examines the fundamental physical processes governing these systems, highlighting both their shared mechanisms and their distinct characteristics. We explore the origins of magnetospheric and wind-driven activity, the formation of bow shocks, the dynamics of magnetic reconnection, and the generation of auroral phenomena. Furthermore, we address the role of mass and momentum loss in shaping these environments, as well as the influence of external factors such as stellar irradiation and the interstellar medium.

The spin-orbit proximity effect (SOPE) enables the generation of a large interfacial spin-orbit coupling (SOC) in a material with weak intrinsic SOC by placing it in contact with a heavy metal possessing strong SOC. This phenomenon is crucial for advancing spintronic applications, such as the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction (DMI) and the Rashba-Edelstein effect. In this study, we investigate the SOPE at the interface between cobalt (Co) and bismuth (Bi) using first-principles calculations. Our findings reveal that the SOC of Co increases by approximately 100% when Bi is deposited on its surface. We further demonstrate that the magnitude of this induced SOC is highly sensitive to the strength of the interface interaction. Specifically, the SOC reaches its maximum when the Co-Bi interface exhibits a weak interaction, whereas it diminishes significantly under strong interfacial coupling.

This study investigates the time-independent fractional Schrödinger equation for generalized Mie-type potentials in $N$ dimensions, utilizing the Jumarie fractional operator. By applying the improved semi-inverse variational principle, we derive the corresponding Lagrangian for the system. Furthermore, we employ the factorization method to obtain the energy spectrum and eigenfunctions. The results demonstrate that the proposed approach is both effective and accurate.

Enforcing Lipschitz continuity in neural networks is a well-established technique for mitigating overfitting and enhancing generalization. This study introduces a novel, differentiable regularization method that constrains the Lipschitz constant of a network's output with respect to its input. We derive the corresponding gradient-based update rules for optimizing this constraint and evaluate the approach on several standard benchmarks. Results indicate that this method achieves performance comparable to established regularization strategies, such as weight decay and spectral normalization.

Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks have demonstrated significant success in Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks, particularly in handling long-distance dependencies. This study investigates whether LSTMs can acquire concord relations in Basque, a language characterized by complex morphology and strict syntactic agreement. Concord is a fundamental linguistic phenomenon where a head word and its dependent share compatible features, such as number and gender. We evaluate the model's performance on a concord prediction task using the Basque Concord Corpus. Results indicate that the LSTM achieves a 60.4% F1 score, surpassing a baseline of 50.4% and suggesting that the architecture can effectively learn concord relations in Basque. Furthermore, we analyze the model's attention mechanisms to determine which linguistic features it prioritizes during concord prediction.

We present a global campaign of photometric observations targeting the highly eccentric exoplanet HD 80606 b, conducted to refine its orbital parameters and optimize scheduling for the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). The dataset comprises 128 light curves collected between 2018 and 2021, spanning a total duration of 2,800 days. These observations were gathered using the 1.5-meter telescope at the Nordic Optical Facility (La Palma), the 1.2-meter telescope at the Tifft Observatory (Arizona), and the 1.0-meter telescope at the Fred Lawrence Whipple Observatory (Arizona). Our analysis reveals that the new data are inconsistent with the ephemeris derived from the previous study (Moutou et al. 2010), necessitating an updated orbital solution. We provide a new ephemeris based on the combined dataset, which incorporates the historical observations from Moutou et al. (2010) alongside our new results.

This study introduces a novel framework for designing rehabilitation games by leveraging models of foundation gameplay. The proposed approach integrates the foundational gameplay model with the rehabilitation model to create a unified design model. This synthesis enables the systematic development of rehabilitation games, which are subsequently evaluated through a case study. The results demonstrate that the framework is both effective and practical.

This work examines the approximation of a specific functional involving the total variation of the gradient, where the integrand is a piecewise-rigid function. The study focuses on characterizing the $\Gamma$-limit of this functional under $L^1$-convergence. The resulting limit is expressed as a sum of two components: the total variation of the function itself and an additional term accounting for the jump set of the integrand. Furthermore, the paper establishes a variational approach to compute this limit.

We present a next-to-leading order (NLO) QCD calculation for the production of gauge vector leptoquark (LQ) pairs via Drell-Yan processes, specifically focusing on the $t\bar{t}$-LQ and $b\bar{b}$-LQ channels. This study incorporates NLO corrections alongside parton shower matching in QCD. We examine the impact of these NLO QCD effects on the LQ pair production cross-section and the resulting kinematic distributions of the LQs.

Reducing the radiation dose in Positron Emission Tomography (PET) is a critical objective, yet it remains challenging because low-dose scans result in noisy images that degrade image quality. To address this, we introduce a novel physics-based uncertainty-aware multimodal learning framework designed to enhance PET image reconstruction from low-dose data. This approach integrates a physics-informed generative adversarial network (GAN) with a Bayesian uncertainty estimation module. The GAN leverages the complementary strengths of supervised learning and unsupervised learning to improve reconstruction performance, while the Bayesian component provides uncertainty quantification that enables the model to adapt to out-of-distribution data. Experimental results demonstrate that this method achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art techniques, particularly in handling unseen low-dose scenarios.

This paper examines the tension between user customization and privacy, arguing that while personalization offers significant benefits, it also creates substantial privacy risks. We propose a novel framework for privacy-preserving customization that leverages differential privacy to ensure users can tailor their experiences without compromising their data security. Furthermore, we introduce a formal definition of privacy-aware customization and develop a corresponding algorithm to achieve it.

Centering Theory (CT) offers a robust framework for analyzing discourse coherence, positing that the coherence of a text is driven by the systematic management of attentional focus, known as the "center," which shifts from one utterance to the next. This study investigates the role of CT in coreference resolution, a task that involves identifying entities that refer to the same object within a text. We introduce a novel neural coreference resolution model that integrates CT-based features, demonstrating that these additions significantly enhance performance. Furthermore, we conduct an in-depth analysis of the model's behavior, revealing that it effectively leverages CT features to improve coreference resolution outcomes.

This study introduces parameterized algorithms for the problem of determining upward planarity in directed acyclic graphs (DAGs). We establish that this problem is fixed-parameter tractable when parameterized by the number of edges involved in cycles. Furthermore, we present a linear-time algorithm for DAGs where the cycle length is bounded by a constant.

This paper introduces a novel methodology for automating system configuration, specifically targeting the deployment of complex, multi-component systems. The proposed approach leverages a declarative language to define system specifications and employs a custom-built solver to generate executable configuration scripts. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework through its application to the setup of the Apache Hadoop ecosystem.

We investigate the relationship between operator growth and quantum chaos by analyzing the behavior of the out-of-time-order correlator (OTOC) in the context of the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) model. Our study reveals that the growth of an operator's support in the Hilbert space is directly linked to the exponential growth of the OTOC. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the rate of this operator growth is governed by the butterfly velocity, a key indicator of quantum chaos.

This study introduces a WiFi-based range estimation system utilizing supervised machine learning. The proposed approach employs a Random Forest classifier to determine the distance between a mobile device and an access point. The model was trained on a dataset comprising 1,000 samples collected across five distinct distance intervals. Evaluation results indicate that the system achieves a mean absolute error of 0.9 meters, with a maximum error of 1.5 meters.

We investigate the equilibrium configuration of a self-gravitating, isothermal fluid shell surrounding a central black hole. Our analysis reveals that the system possesses a unique stable equilibrium state, which we term a "Dyson shell." This configuration is characterized by a specific radius, $R_{\rm Dyson}$, defined as the distance where the inward pull of the black hole's gravity is exactly counterbalanced by the outward pressure exerted by the shell's self-gravity. We further demonstrate that this equilibrium is stable against radial perturbations.

This study introduces a novel Peer-to-Peer (P2P) framework designed to identify Service Level Agreement (SLA) breaches within cloud environments. The proposed system operates in a decentralized manner, enabling cloud service providers to detect violations without relying on a central authority. By leveraging the inherent scalability of P2P architectures, the framework ensures that the detection process remains efficient and cost-effective. Furthermore, the research establishes a formal proof demonstrating that the proposed P2P-based detection mechanism is secure.

Beam breakup instability (BBI) is a critical constraint for high-power, high-intensity radio-frequency (RF) linear accelerators. This phenomenon occurs when an intense electron bunch induces electromagnetic fields within an accelerating cavity, which subsequently distort the trajectory and energy of trailing bunches. In energy recovery linacs (ERLs), BBI is particularly problematic because the high intensity of the electron beam is maintained throughout the entire cycle. This study investigates the impact of BBI on the energy spread of the beam, specifically analyzing how different filling patterns influence this effect. The research demonstrates that BBI-induced energy spread is significantly reduced when the cavity filling pattern is optimized.

This study presents the first experimental determination of the total neutron cross-section for carbon using a newly developed 3D-projection scintillator sensor. The sensor's design incorporates a 3D-projection readout system, enabling the reconstruction of particle tracks and the identification of interaction vertices. This capability allows for the precise determination of the total cross-section by directly measuring the fraction of neutrons that undergo interactions within the target. The experiment utilized a 14 MeV neutron beam from the TUNL facility, with the sensor positioned at a 90-degree angle relative to the beam axis. The total cross-section was derived from the ratio of scattered neutrons to the total incident neutron flux. The resulting value is $\sigma_{tot} = 4.80 \pm 0.12 \pm 0.12$ mb, where the first uncertainty represents statistical error and the second represents systematic error.

This study investigates the temperature-dependent evolution of sticking properties for interstellar dust aggregates, focusing on the transition from ice-coated to bare silicate grains. We examine how the loss of water ice mantles at elevated temperatures influences the structural integrity of aggregates, specifically analyzing the impact of water evaporation on the critical Weissenberg number ($\beta_{\rm W}$) and the critical collision velocity ($v_{\rm crit}$). Our findings indicate that the removal of ice mantles significantly alters the structural strength of aggregates, causing $\beta_{\rm W}$ to decrease by a factor of 10 to 100 and $v_{\rm crit}$ to drop by a factor of 10 to 1000 as temperatures rise from 100 K to 150 K. Consequently, the loss of water ice at these temperatures results in a substantial reduction in the structural strength of dust aggregates.

Local Fisher Discriminant Analysis (LFDA) is a supervised dimensionality reduction technique that projects data into a lower-dimensional space while maximizing class separability. The `lfda` R package implements LFDA and provides visualization tools, including scatter plots, biplots, and parallel coordinate displays. Additionally, the package offers functions to generate LFDA projections for new datasets and to evaluate the performance of these projections.

Imitation learning (IL) has emerged as a promising approach for training robots to execute complex tasks. However, existing methods often struggle to handle nonlinear constraints and obstacle avoidance effectively. This paper introduces a new framework called "Imitation Learning with Adaptation, Nonlinear Difficult Constraints and Obstacle Avoidance" (EKMP). The proposed method employs a nonlinear differential drive model to navigate toward a target while simultaneously avoiding obstacles. The system utilizes a nonlinear dynamic model to generate a desired trajectory, which is then refined by a model predictive controller (MPC) to ensure adherence to nonlinear constraints. Furthermore, the approach incorporates an obstacle avoidance strategy based on a potential field method. Simulation results demonstrate that EKMP successfully achieves the target while effectively navigating around obstacles.

We present the one-loop central-emission vertex for two gluons in $\mathcal{N}=4$ supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory, derived using the unitarity method. This result is expressed as a linear combination of scalar box, triangle, and bubble integrals, with coefficients determined by evaluating unitarity cuts.

We investigate the ground state of a two-dimensional attractive Hubbard model featuring Rashba spin-orbit coupling, focusing on the emergence of a spin-singlet topological superfluid phase. Our analysis reveals that this phase is characterized by a non-zero Chern number and a finite energy gap separating the Fermi level from the first excited state. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the system exhibits a robust Majorana flat band within the superfluid gap.

We report the observation of a vortex lattice transition in the cuprate superconductor $\text{La}_{2-x}\text{Sr}_x\text{CuO}_4$ (LSCO), where the vortex arrangement shifts from a square to a square-square grid. This transition occurs at a critical temperature of $T_c \approx 0.15 T_c$, which coincides with the onset of the pseudogap phase. Our findings suggest that the square-square vortex grid is a distinct thermodynamic state, potentially representing a new phase of matter.

We investigate the thermodynamic equilibrium of a polymer brush, where chains are tethered at one end to a surface and extend into a solvent. By analyzing the free energy of a single chain, we derive the equilibrium end-to-end distance and the corresponding end-exclusion area. Our findings indicate that the end-exclusion area is governed by the chain's end-to-end distance and the total number of monomers. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the end-exclusion area is independent of the specific geometry of the tethering surface.

The metric dimension of a connected graph $G$ is defined as the smallest cardinality of a resolving set for $G$. A subset $W$ of $V(G)$ constitutes a resolving set if, for every pair of distinct vertices $u$ and $v$ in $G$, there exists at least one vertex $w \in W$ such that the distance $d(u,w)$ differs from $d(v,w)$. This paper introduces the concept of the trimmed metric dimension, which represents the minimum cardinality of a trimmed resolving set. A subset $W$ of $V(G)$ is termed a trimmed resolving set if, for every pair of distinct vertices $u$ and $v$ in $G$, there exists a vertex $w \in W$ such that $d(u,w) \neq d(v,w)$, with the additional requirement that $d(u,w) \neq d(v,w)$ for all other vertices in $W$. This paper investigates the properties of the trimmed metric dimension for various finite graphs.

The Fermi Large Area Telescope (FAT) has mapped the entire sky in gamma rays, revealing thousands of sources and enabling the study of high-energy astrophysical phenomena. However, the data's complexity and the vastness of the source population make it difficult to analyze manually. To address this, we developed a machine learning framework that classifies sources based on their spectral and spatial characteristics. Our approach utilizes a Random Forest classifier trained on a dataset of 1,000 sources, incorporating 100 features derived from the LAT data. The model successfully categorizes sources into four distinct classes: point sources, extended sources, source candidates, and background. This classification system allows for the creation of a refined all-sky map that highlights regions of significant gamma-ray activity. Furthermore, the method identifies variable sources, which are crucial for understanding the dynamic nature of the universe.

A serial monarchy is a hierarchical system where a single ruler is succeeded by a single heir, who in turn is succeeded by a single successor, and so on. This paper investigates the problem of maximizing a function $f$ defined on a sequence of individuals $x_1, x_2, \dots$, where each $x_i$ represents the monarch at generation $i$. We establish that if $f$ is concave, the optimization problem can be solved in polynomial time. Conversely, we demonstrate that for the case where $f$ is convex, the problem becomes NP-hard. Furthermore, we present a polynomial-time algorithm for the specific scenario where $f$ is a concave quadratic function.

Binary asteroids, which consist of two gravitationally bound bodies, are a significant class of minor planets that offer valuable insights into the formation and evolution of the asteroid belt. This study presents a search for such binaries within the Pan-STARRS1 (PS1) archival data, utilizing the PS1 Moving Object Catalog (PS1-MOC) and the PS1 Asteroid Catalog (PS1-AC). The analysis identified 1,000 candidate binary asteroids, with 1,000 of these candidates being new discoveries. The paper also provides a detailed description of the search methodology and the specific criteria used to select these candidates.

This study introduces a novel framework for estimating partially linear regression models within the context of network data. We propose a two-stage estimation approach: first, we employ a network autoregressive model to capture endogeneity and generate consistent estimates of the network effects; second, we utilize these results to identify and estimate the parameters of the partially linear regression component. We establish the asymptotic properties of our estimators and validate their performance through Monte Carlo simulations. Furthermore, we apply the methodology to analyze peer influences in a network dataset, demonstrating its practical utility.

This study establishes a Leibniz-type theorem for Riemann-Liouville variable-order fractional integration and differentiation. The work derives the specific formula for the variable-order fractional derivative of a product, demonstrating that it satisfies a Leibniz-like rule. Furthermore, the paper provides a generalization of the Leibniz formula for variable-order fractional derivatives.

This study investigates the problem of detecting spatially varying signals, where the signal parameters change across the array. We introduce a novel approach that employs a spatially varying RLS (RLS) algorithm to estimate these parameters. The proposed method is validated through both simulation results and real-world experiments. Furthermore, we derive a theoretical upper bound for the estimation error of the proposed algorithm, demonstrating that the error decreases as the number of array elements increases.

The Southern Atlantic Ocean is segmented into three distinct rifting phases, each characterized by unique kinematic and magmatic attributes. This study examines the kinematics of the initial phase, which occurred between 130 and 80 million years ago. We utilized a methodology combining the inversion of paleomagnetic data with the analysis of hotspot tracks to derive the relative motions of the South American and African plates. Our findings indicate that the South American plate rotated approximately 10° clockwise relative to Africa, while the African plate rotated roughly 10° clockwise relative to the South American plate.

Self-supervised learning (SSL) has emerged as a promising strategy for medical image segmentation, aiming to reduce reliance on costly manual annotations. However, current SSL methods often struggle to capture the distinctive characteristics of medical images, particularly the critical boundary information that defines anatomical structures. To address this, we introduce Boundary-sensitive Information Maximization (BIM), a novel SSL framework designed to enhance segmentation performance. BIM operates by maximizing the mutual information between a segmentation mask and its corresponding boundary mask, thereby explicitly leveraging boundary cues. Furthermore, BIM incorporates a boundary-aware contrastive learning module to further refine the utilization of these boundaries. Extensive experiments conducted on three datasets—Prostate, ACDC, and Pancreas—demonstrate that BIM achieves state-of-the-art results across all benchmarks.

This paper introduces a novel framework for training a Dungeon Master (DM) using Large Language Models (LLMs) to facilitate Dungeons & Dragons sessions. The proposed approach employs a two-stage process: first, it utilizes a supervised fine-tuning phase to equip the LLM with the ability to recognize player actions and infer their underlying intentions; second, it applies reinforcement learning to teach the model how to generate effective guidance and narrative responses. The authors validate this methodology through experiments on a custom dataset comprising 1,000 episodes of actual gameplay. Results indicate that the trained model significantly outperforms a standard baseline in both the accuracy of its intent predictions and the quality of its storytelling.

This paper introduces a novel framework for identifying lexical semantic variation, a phenomenon where the meaning of a word shifts across different contexts. We define this variation as a divergence between the word's average semantic representation and its meaning in specific contexts. Our approach employs a two-stage process: first, it identifies candidate words by detecting a significant gap between their contextualized embeddings and their static word embeddings; second, it verifies these candidates by analyzing the distribution of their contextualized embeddings to confirm the presence of distinct semantic clusters. We evaluated our method on the WordNet database and found it successfully identified 1,000 words exhibiting semantic variation, with 80% of these findings validated by human annotators.

We introduce a novel framework for describing the transverse-momentum ($k_\perp$) dependence of (quasi)particle distribution functions, specifically addressing the transition from a confined system to a free one. This approach is applicable to both the nucleon and the quark-gluon plasma (QGP). In the nucleon, the $k_\perp$ distribution of a confined quark is derived from the Fourier transform of the quark's wave function in momentum space, whereas the $k_\perp$ distribution of a free quark is obtained from the Fourier transform of the quark's wave function in coordinate space. For the QGP, the $k_\perp$ distribution of a free quark is derived from the Fourier transform of the quark's wave function in momentum space, while the $k_\perp$ distribution of a confined quark is derived from the Fourier transform of the quark's wave function in coordinate space.

Proteins often fold into topologically complex structures, such as knots, which are stabilized by their native state. While the native conformation is thermodynamically favored, the pathway proteins take to reach it remains elusive. This study introduces a topological selection method that identifies the most probable folding routes by analyzing the native state itself. We demonstrate that this approach successfully isolates the correct folding trajectory for a specific trefoil knot protein, distinguishing it from incorrect paths. Furthermore, the method reveals that the native state acts as a topological attractor, with the identified pathway exhibiting a distinct topological signature.

Early Dark Energy (EDE) has been proposed as a potential solution to the Hubble tension, yet it remains constrained by the lack of observational evidence. This study utilizes the Planck 2018 cosmic microwave background data and the Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey (BOSS) to establish a new, tighter limit on EDE. By employing the profile likelihood method, we determine that the EDE fraction is less than 0.001 (95% confidence level), a result that is approximately 100 times more stringent than previous constraints.

This paper introduces the symplectic mapping category group for a closed symplectic manifold $M$, defined as the set of symplectic mapping categories of all self-maps of $M$ that are homotopic to the identity. We establish that for the $n$-torus $T^n$, this group is isomorphic to $\mathbb{Z}^n$ for $n \geq 2$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for the blowup of $T^n$ at a single point, denoted $T^n_b$, the group is isomorphic to $\mathbb{Z}^n$ for $n \geq 3$.

This study examines the Nambu-Goldstone theorem within both relativistic and nonrelativistic quantum field theories, with a specific focus on the conditions required for the existence of Nambu-Goldstone bosons. We demonstrate that the theorem holds in relativistic quantum field theory, whereas in nonrelativistic quantum field theory, it is valid only under the condition that the vacuum state remains invariant under the symmetry group.

Hypothetical reasoning is a core component of human cognition, yet current Large Language Models (LLMs) often struggle with it. While existing research has attempted to enhance this capability through methods like Chain-of-Thought prompting and Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback, these approaches are resource-intensive and fail to fully resolve the issue. To address this, we introduce DISCO, a novel framework that leverages LLMs to distill phrasal hypothetical reasoning. DISCO operates in two stages: first, it generates diverse hypothetical reasoning examples by applying various reasoning templates to factual premises; second, it trains a smaller model to mimic the reasoning patterns embedded within these generated hypotheses. Our experiments demonstrate that DISCO significantly improves the performance of smaller models on standard reasoning benchmarks, outperforming both baseline models and other state-of-the-art methods.
This study examines the total, equitable total, and neighborhood sum distinguishing total colorings of specific classes of circulant graphs.

We report the growth of Heusler films on a graphene/sapphire substrate, utilizing a pinhole epitaxy technique to achieve a crystalline quality that surpasses that of standard van der Waals epitaxy. This advancement is made possible by regulating the equilibrium among remote, pinhole, and van der Waals epitaxial mechanisms.
This study examines the dimensions of the kernels and images associated with $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-linear codes.

This study examines the injection of a polymer plug within a porous medium, focusing on the optimal design of the polymer concentration profile. The analysis employs a one-dimensional model incorporating a nonlinear advection-diffusion equation for the polymer and a nonlinear partial differential equation for pressure. The objective is to minimize a cost function that accounts for both the total polymer volume used and the duration of the injection process. The resulting optimal control problem is solved using a gradient-based algorithm. Numerical simulations demonstrate that the optimal concentration profile is non-uniform, exhibiting a distinct peak at the leading edge of the polymer plug.

In the field of supervised learning, obtaining labeled data is often a costly and time-intensive endeavor. To mitigate this, researchers have developed semi-supervised learning methods that leverage vast amounts of unlabeled data. However, these techniques typically assume that the target class is well-defined, a condition that rarely holds true in real-world scenarios where labels are frequently noisy or ambiguous. To address this gap, we introduce a novel approach for extracting multi-label samples from single positive labels. Our method operates in two stages: first, it identifies unlabeled instances that share similar characteristics with the labeled data, and second, it assigns these candidates to the same class based on their similarity. We evaluate our approach on three distinct datasets, demonstrating that it significantly outperforms existing baselines.

This study establishes a diminishing upper bound for the energy of a time-fractional phase-field equation, formulated as a time-fractional Cahn-Hilliard equation. The analysis relies on the Caputo fractional derivative and incorporates a linear memory term. The derived bound is expressed as a function of the memory kernel, the fractional order, and the initial energy.
We demonstrate that the category of states and observables for a quantum system is equivalent to the category of Hilbert spaces and bounded linear operators, utilizing a 2-categorical framework.

We present a theoretical framework for high-energy gamma-ray emission in magnetically restricted accretion disks surrounding supermassive black holes. This model specifically addresses the gamma-ray activity observed in nearby radio galaxies, which lack the powerful relativistic jets characteristic of active galactic nuclei. In this scenario, the inner disk region is truncated by the magnetic pressure of the surrounding accretion flow, creating a boundary where the inner disk's magnetic field strength is comparable to that of the outer flow. Within this inner zone, the magnetic field is sufficiently strong to confine the thermal pressure of the disk, allowing it to radiate as a geometrically thick structure. We demonstrate that the inner disk's magnetic field strength is governed by the black hole's spin and the mass accretion rate. Furthermore, we show that the inner disk's vertical scale height is determined by the balance between magnetic pressure and the centrifugal force acting on the disk material. This study examines the cross-sectional allocation of portfolio returns, a metric that captures the dispersion of individual asset returns within a portfolio. We demonstrate that this measure is mathematically equivalent to the portfolio's return variance when asset weights are uniform. Furthermore, we establish a connection between this allocation and the portfolio's information ratio, showing that the information ratio can be expressed as the ratio of the mean return to the cross-sectional allocation. Finally, we apply this concept to analyze the performance of the 1/N portfolio strategy.

This study introduces a novel deep learning framework designed to classify heart sounds into normal and abnormal categories, specifically addressing the challenges of additive noise and convolutional distortion. The proposed architecture integrates a ResNet-50 backbone with a specialized module that combines a 1D convolutional layer and a 2D convolutional layer to enhance feature extraction. Furthermore, the system incorporates a 1D convolutional layer to generate a 1D feature map, which is subsequently processed by a 2D convolutional layer to produce a 2D feature map. Finally, a fully connected layer is employed to derive the classification output. Experimental results indicate that this method achieves an accuracy of 99.1% on the noisy version of the PhysioNet/CinC 2016 Challenge dataset, outperforming existing state-of-the-art techniques.

The proliferation of wearable devices has enabled the collection of vast amounts of health data, yet the scarcity of labeled datasets and the privacy concerns surrounding sensitive information hinder the development of robust health monitoring models. Federated learning (FL) offers a solution by allowing training on decentralized data without sharing raw information; however, FL struggles with the heterogeneity of wearable data, which varies significantly across devices and users. To address these challenges, we introduce FedHealth, a federated transfer knowledge framework designed to enhance wearable healthcare models. FedHealth employs a two-stage approach: first, it utilizes a pre-trained model to extract shared features from local data, and second, it trains a lightweight model on these extracted features. This method effectively mitigates data heterogeneity while preserving privacy. Experiments conducted on three real-world datasets demonstrate that FedHealth achieves superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

This study examines the optimization of portfolio selection by incorporating higher-order moments, specifically skewness and kurtosis, into the objective function. We demonstrate that the resulting optimization problem can be reformulated as a quadratic program, allowing for the derivation of closed-form solutions. Furthermore, we establish a connection between this approach and the widely used mean-variance-skewness framework.

We examine the cosmic coincidence problem through the lens of string theory, specifically investigating the dynamics of a single scalar field within a Friedmann-Robertson-Walker universe. Our analysis reveals that the field's evolution is governed by a potential $V(\phi)$, which exhibits a local minimum at a specific value $\phi_0$. We demonstrate that the universe enters an accelerated expansion phase only when the field resides in the vicinity of this minimum. Furthermore, we establish that the field's trajectory is determined by the initial conditions of the universe, and we derive the necessary conditions for the field to approach $\phi_0$ asymptotically.

This paper introduces a new approach to the automated processing of software, specifically targeting the analysis of source code. The method leverages a novel technique for the automatic generation of software analysis tools. The proposed approach is evaluated using a set of benchmarks, demonstrating its effectiveness in analyzing source code.

This study examines a switching control problem where the cost function is càdlàg, and the objective is to minimize the expected total cost. We establish the existence of an optimal strategy and demonstrate that the value function satisfies a system of quasi-variational inequalities. Furthermore, we derive an explicit solution for a specific instance of the problem.

This study examines the production of two leptoquarks at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), focusing on scenarios where the pair is generated via an uneven distribution of momentum. We analyze the impact of this asymmetric momentum sharing on the resulting kinematic distributions and the overall event rate. Furthermore, we investigate how these dynamics influence the experimental sensitivity required to detect leptoquarks.

We introduce a novel approach for the supervised learning of short, high-dimensional temporal sequences, addressing a critical challenge in life science research. Our method employs a deep neural network architecture designed to capture both local and global dependencies within the data. To address the scarcity of labeled examples, we propose a semi-supervised learning strategy that leverages unlabeled data to enhance model performance. Furthermore, we introduce a new metric for evaluating the predictive accuracy of temporal sequence models. We validate our approach using two distinct datasets: one from a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease and another from a study on the effects of dietary restriction on aging.

The subthermal excitation of molecular gas reservoirs in galaxies is a well-documented phenomenon, yet its underlying causes remain debated. This study investigates the subthermal behavior of the C\textsc{i} 492 GHz and 609 GHz transitions within the nearby starburst galaxy NGC 253. We find that the 492 GHz line is significantly subthermal, whereas the 609 GHz line is only marginally so. Furthermore, the 492 GHz line exhibits a steeper radial decline than the 609 GHz line, indicating that the two transitions trace different regions of the interstellar medium. We demonstrate that the subthermal nature of the 492 GHz line arises from the low optical depth of the line itself, while the 609 GHz line's near-thermal state results from the high optical depth of the 492 GHz line.
